report.businessDescription: Alphabet’s principal earnings engine is Google Services (advertising plus subscriptions, platforms and devices), supplemented by Google Cloud’s consumption/subscription infrastructure and platform offerings; Other Bets remains immaterial and loss-making. In the six months ended June 30, 2026, Google Services generated $184,177 million of revenue and $80,133 million of operating income, while Google Cloud generated $44,796 million of revenue and $15,412 million of operating income. Cloud growth was driven primarily by infrastructure and platform services, with TPU-system revenue beginning in Q2 2026. The economic trade-off is an unusually large AI-compute buildout: cash capital expenditures were $80,598 million in the first half of 2026, principally technical infrastructure, while depreciation on property and equipment was $13,600 million. The company also uses committed and uncommenced data-center leases alongside cash capex. [S1]
uncertainties: The forecast uses the June 30, 2026 trailing-twelve-month base supplied by the user; Alphabet had not filed a September 30, 2026 Form 10-Q as of October 22, 2026 in the supplied filing set.

Management said it expects a significant 2026 increase in technical-infrastructure investment, but did not disclose an annual cash-capex dollar target or a dated revenue-growth outlook; forecast capex and revenue assumptions are analyst estimates. [S1, S3]

Depreciation is rising behind the AI infrastructure deployment, but the useful lives, placement-in-service timing, and mix of servers versus data-center construction make the future D&A/revenue path uncertain. [S1]

Google Cloud’s reported 2026 growth includes newly recognized TPU-system sales; the recurring versus hardware component, unit volumes, pricing, customer concentration, and contract duration are undisclosed. [S1]
The June 2026 equity, mandatory-convertible preferred, and potential $40,000 million ATM issuance create material uncertainty around future dilution; the forecast does not model share count. [S1]

The company has $85,200 million of leases not yet commenced, primarily data centers, plus a $5,800 million short-term lease commitment commencing in Q3 2026. These are not treated as cash capex in the forecast’s capex ratio. [S1]

A recent observable USD senior-unsecured bond yield with 7-13 years remaining could not be independently verified from a primary market source; observedDebtYield and bond maturity fields are therefore null.

stressRationale.explanation: The stress case assumes advertising and Cloud demand slow while AI infrastructure depreciation, technical-infrastructure usage costs, content acquisition costs and TAC remain comparatively sticky. A 23.0% EBIT margin is substantially below the 33.1% trailing base, but remains above a severe break-even outcome because Google Services and Cloud were both profitable in the latest reported half-year.

bondRationale.explanation: No qualifying recent USD senior-unsecured 7-13-year secondary-market yield was verified from a primary source. The latest 10-Q does establish that Alphabet’s notes are senior unsecured and rank equally, and that USD notes issued in 2026 mature from 2029 to 2066, but it does not report market yields.

liquidityRationale.explanation: At June 30, 2026, cash and short-term marketable securities were substantial, the company stated those resources plus operating cash flow and financing activities should fund commitments for at least 12 months and thereafter for the foreseeable future, and it had $11,700 million of credit facilities through April 2030. Offsetting factors are exceptionally high AI capex, lease commitments, $101,085 million face value of long-term debt, and announced potential ATM issuance.

hFactors.explanation: Advertising is cyclical and Cloud consumption can soften with customer usage; however, Q2 2026 revenue growth was broad-based and the company has diversified advertising, subscription, cloud, and hardware-related revenue streams.
hFactors.name: Demand drop

hFactors.explanation: Alphabet identifies intense competition, including from developers and providers of AI products and services. Search, AI assistants, digital advertising, hyperscale cloud, and enterprise AI all face credible well-capitalized competitors.
hFactors.name: Competitive attack

hFactors.explanation: Technical infrastructure depends on servers, networking equipment, data-center construction and leased capacity. Alphabet is scaling these inputs rapidly, but reports no singular supplier dependency that would imply acute supplier-loss risk.
hFactors.name: Loss of suppliers

hFactors.explanation: The AI buildout requires scarce technical and research talent, but Alphabet had 198,933 employees at June 30, 2026 and a large global recruiting and compensation base; loss-of-employee risk is meaningful rather than existential.
hFactors.name: Loss of employees

hFactors.explanation: Data centers, servers and network equipment are specialized long-lived assets. Their resale value could be impaired by technology change, but Alphabet has high ongoing internal demand and substantial liquidity, lowering forced-sale likelihood.
hFactors.name: Asset fire sales

hFactors.explanation: Alphabet’s direct digital products are distributed online rather than through a concentrated physical dealer network. Traffic-acquisition partners and device/platform relationships matter, but classic dealer loss is limited.
hFactors.name: Loss of dealers

hFactors.explanation: Alphabet accessed public debt, equity, a private placement, mandatory convertible preferred funding, credit facilities and an ATM program during 2026. Capital-market access is therefore strong, although the breadth of financing highlights the scale of AI infrastructure commitments.
hFactors.name: Loss of capital markets

businessDrivers.description: Google advertising remains the largest revenue pool within Google Services; its results depend on user engagement, advertiser demand, query/product quality, pricing and traffic-acquisition economics. Alphabet does not report a single consolidated advertising unit-volume or price metric.
businessDrivers.name: Google advertising demand and monetization

businessDrivers.description: Paid subscriptions across YouTube services and Google One drove subscriptions, platforms and devices growth in the latest reported half-year; subscriber counts and ARPU are not disclosed in the filing.
businessDrivers.name: Subscription expansion

businessDrivers.description: Google Cloud growth was led by infrastructure and platform services, including enterprise AI infrastructure, Vertex AI, Gemini Enterprise, cybersecurity, and data and analytics offerings.
businessDrivers.name: Cloud infrastructure and AI consumption

businessDrivers.description: Q2 2026 was the first quarter in which Alphabet recognized revenue from sales of TPU systems; the future contribution is uncertain because customer volumes, pricing and recurrence are undisclosed.
businessDrivers.name: TPU-system product sales

businessDrivers.description: Cash capex is predominantly servers, networking equipment, data-center land and construction. Management expects 2026 technical-infrastructure investment to increase significantly from 2025.
businessDrivers.name: AI technical-infrastructure investment

businessDrivers.description: New infrastructure raises depreciation after assets enter service; construction and assembly can span months to years, so the P&L burden lags cash capex.
businessDrivers.name: Depreciation ramp and asset utilization

businessDrivers.description: Google Services profitability benefits from revenue growth but is partly offset by TAC; Cloud profitability is partly offset by technical-infrastructure usage costs and employee compensation.
businessDrivers.name: Revenue mix, TAC, and infrastructure operating costs

businessDrivers.description: Alphabet-level activities include centralized AI research and development, which is not allocated to operating segments and can constrain consolidated margin as frontier-model investment continues.
businessDrivers.name: Central AI research expense

businessDrivers.description: Capacity is supplemented by operating and finance leases, including large uncommenced data-center leases; lease commitments are distinct from cash purchases of property and equipment.
businessDrivers.name: Data-center lease capacity

businessDrivers.description: Competition from AI product and service developers, platform regulation, and legal settlements can affect traffic, distribution, billing practices, fees, and business models.
businessDrivers.name: Competition and regulation

marginRationale.explanation: The estimate begins below the trailing 33.1% EBIT margin because the ongoing AI buildout increases depreciation, technical-infrastructure usage costs and centralized AI research. Margin then stabilizes near 31.5%-32.0% as Cloud scale, Google Services monetization and higher utilization offset part of the cost burden. This does not assume that the current TTM margin fully persists: Google Cloud’s latest operating-profit growth was accompanied by higher infrastructure and compensation costs, and Alphabet disclosed rising TAC in Google Services.

terminalRationale.explanation: A 4.0% terminal growth assumption reflects a mature global advertising and enterprise-compute franchise, not perpetual AI hypergrowth. The 31.0% terminal margin and 25.0% ROIC allow for durable advantages from distribution, search/ads data and software platforms, while recognizing persistent AI infrastructure reinvestment, depreciation and intense competition. Negative operating working capital is retained but moderated because advertising and subscriptions generate favorable cash timing, whereas a larger enterprise-cloud and hardware mix requires more receivables, inventory and support commitments.

growthRationale.explanation: Year 1 retains elevated growth because the TTM base includes strong Cloud infrastructure/platform demand, rising paid subscriptions, and initial TPU-system revenue. Growth decelerates each year as the revenue base expands and the TPU introduction annualizes. The forecast does not assign unreported Cloud units, AI query volumes, advertising price, or subscription ARPU; it is anchored instead in disclosed revenue streams, Cloud demand drivers, and management’s continuing infrastructure commitment.

investmentRationale.explanation: Cash capex/revenue remains very high in years 1-2 because management expects a significant 2026 increase versus 2025 and reported $80,598 million of first-half 2026 cash capex. It declines thereafter as the initial AI capacity wave is placed in service and utilization rises, but remains above Alphabet’s pre-2025 pattern because Cloud and AI workloads require continuing server, network and data-center investment. Finance-lease principal and undiscounted operating-lease commitments are not included in cash capex.

modelRationale.explanation: FCFF is appropriate because Alphabet is a non-financial operating company with material operating income, cash flow from operations, technical-infrastructure capex, working-capital balances and conventional senior unsecured debt. Its 2026 financing activity and data-center lease commitments require separate financing review, but do not make it a bank, insurer, or REIT.

Amazon is comparable through hyperscale cloud capacity, AI infrastructure and a meaningful advertising business. Its first-party retail, logistics and inventory intensity make its consolidated margin and working-capital profile materially different.
